documents.unit: Office of the Provost (University Academic Regulations)
documents.title: Code of Academic Integrity (University Academic Regulations, Bulletin 2026-2027)
documents.stance_why: A coded restrict, B coded delegates. Source: unauthorized AI use is listed as misuse ('accessing or using AI tools without authorization'), but the code never says who authorizes or what is allowed, and it states 'What constitutes use or misuse of AI will differ depending on context and discipline' and refers to the instructor's written 'Course AI Policy'. The document sets no default permit or ban of its own and hands the decision to courses, so delegates; A's restrict reading would need a stated default that the text does not give.
documents.summary: The University of Portland's academic integrity code adds 'Misuse of AI' as a fourth violation category beside cheating, forgery and plagiarism, naming undisclosed AI-generated work, unauthorized AI use and unacknowledged AI contributions. The rest is the general penalty levels and reporting, review and appeal process, which now applies to AI cases; the faculty member must supply the written 'Course AI Policy' when reporting an AI violation.

units.why: The sentence classes AI misuse as an integrity violation 'comparable to cheating or plagiarism', which is the P36 move of treating improper AI use as misconduct; it binds everyone in the community, so actor is all.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P36, actor all and phase when-misuse; they differed on modality (A informs, B must-not). The source says AI misuse 'is considered a violation of academic integrity comparable to cheating or plagiarism', which classes the act as misconduct and thereby forbids it, so must-not. B's normalized policy is faithful to the sentence and is kept because the anchor lacks the subject.
units.anchor: considered a violation of academic integrity comparable to cheating or plagiarism
units.frag_start: The misuse of artificial intelligence
units.policy: The misuse of AI to circumvent learning goals or to engage in research misconduct is considered a violation of academic integrity comparable to cheating or plagiarism.

units.why: The sentence scopes the AI clause: misuse 'to circumvent learning goals or to engage in research misconduct'. It sets what the clause covers, so P61. Both halves are one definition of misuse, so one unit.
units.resolution_why: A coded one scope unit (P61); B split it into P41 (learning rationale) and P62 (research). Source: the phrase 'circumvent learning goals' only names what misuse defeats and develops no skill-building argument, so P41 does not fit; 'research misconduct' is part of the same definition and the AI-misuse-as-violation rule is already in the P36 unit, so P62 is not a separate rule. Final: one P61 unit, with B's P41 and P62 observations kept in fit_note.
units.anchor: misuse of artificial intelligence technologies (AI) to circumvent learning goals
units.frag_start: The misuse of artificial intelligence
units.fit_note: Also names research misconduct as a covered kind of misuse, which P61 does not capture. Coder B read the 'circumvent learning goals' half as a learning rationale (P41, partial fit: no skill-building argument is developed) and the 'research misconduct' half as P62 (partial fit: no theses, manuscripts or venue rules are named).

units.why: It says 'What constitutes use or misuse of AI will differ depending on context and discipline', so the line is not fixed centrally. P04 (setting varies by instructor/assignment) is nearest; P109 (aligning with discipline norms) does not fit since nobody is told to coordinate.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P04, actor all, phase general, informs. A's anchor includes the full sentence; kept. Both noted that context and discipline, not named instructors, decide, so the fit_note stands.
units.anchor: What constitutes use or misuse of AI will differ depending on context and discipline.
units.frag_start: What constitutes use or misuse
units.fit_note: Says context and discipline decide, not specifically the instructor or assignment.

units.why: Item [1] makes 'submitting work generated by AI as one's own without proper acknowledgement' a violation. The wrongdoing is defined by missing acknowledgement, so this is a disclosure rule (P24) rather than P19, which would ban AI-produced work outright.
units.resolution_why: A coded P19 (ban on passing off AI-generated work), B coded P24 (acknowledgement). Source: '[1] submitting work generated by AI as one's own without proper acknowledgement'. The wrong is the missing acknowledgement and claiming authorship; the text does not ban AI-generated work that is acknowledged, so P19 (do not have AI produce the work you submit) overstates it. P24 is the closer fit. Modality stays must-not and unit_stance restrict, as both coders had.
units.anchor: submitting work generated by AI as one’s own without proper acknowledgement
units.frag_start: submitting work generated by AI
units.fit_note: Also makes passing off AI work as one's own a violation; the text does not say whether acknowledged AI work is acceptable.

units.why: The second example, 'accessing or using AI tools without authorization', makes AI use misuse unless authorized. That is an authorization-required rule (P107) rather than a tier or a syllabus-silence rule.
units.resolution_why: A coded P107 (prior approval), B coded P06 (fallback when a syllabus is silent). Source: '[2] accessing or using AI tools without authorization' makes authorization a precondition for AI use. That is the prior-approval rule of P107. P06 concerns what applies when a syllabus says nothing, and the passage does not mention a syllabus. Both noted the text does not say who authorizes.
units.anchor: accessing or using AI tools without authorization
units.frag_start: accessing or using AI tools
units.fit_note: Does not say who authorizes (the 'Course AI Policy' later suggests the instructor).

units.why: Item [3] makes 'failure to acknowledge AI-generated contributions' itself a violation, which is P28 (nondisclosure is the violation). I chose P28 over P24 because the unit names failure to disclose as the offence, not a duty to disclose.
units.resolution_why: A coded P24 (must, require), B coded P28 (must-not, restrict). Source: '[3] failure to acknowledge AI-generated contributions to an assignment or other academic work' is listed as misuse, so nondisclosure is itself the violation (P28). The positive duty to disclose is P24 and is already coded from item [1]. Final P28, must-not, restrict.
units.anchor: failure to acknowledge AI-generated contributions to an assignment or other academic work
units.frag_start: failure to acknowledge AI-generated contributions
units.fit_note: P28 also covers making disclosure safe; the passage only names nondisclosure as the violation and gives no format or grading effect.

units.why: The code tells students to 'consult directly with their teachers' for more precise information; AI is among the examples. Closest is P10 (ask before using), though the sentence is about all violations, not AI use specifically.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P10, student, course-start, should. The sentence is generic across integrity violations, as both fit_notes say.
units.anchor: Students should consult directly with their teachers.
units.frag_start: Students should consult directly with
units.fit_note: Applies to all integrity violations, not only AI, and is about asking for precise information, not about uncertain uses.

units.why: It says 'Ignorance of these or other breaches of academic integrity will not be deemed ... an excuse', so students must learn the rules (P78) or be held responsible. It covers AI because the AI clause is among the examples. P78 fits only partly, since it is generic.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. Source: 'Ignorance of these or other breaches of academic integrity will not be deemed by the University as an excuse for failure to meet its expectations.' It is a real rule that applies to AI misuse as one listed breach, so kept; P78 fits partly.

units.frag_start: Ignorance of these or other
units.fit_note: Generic across all integrity violations; stated as a no-excuse rule rather than a duty to read course rules.

units.why: The sentence sets the factors for choosing a penalty: 'knowledge-level and experience', 'degree of intention', and whether this is a first offense. This is closest to P37 on penalties; P69 (evidence standards) is about proof, not penalty.
units.resolution_why: Both coded P37, admin, when-misuse, should, neutral, from the same sentence (A anchored on the first/repeat clause, B on the knowledge-level clause). Source: 'consideration should be given to the knowledge-level and experience ..., the degree of intention ..., the nature of the violation, and whether or not this is a first offense or a repeat offense'. Merged to one unit with B's wider anchor; it lists factors for penalty choice, as both fit_notes say.

units.why: The sentence assigns penalty decisions: 'at the discretion of the provost and dean or their designees'. It names who decides penalties, so P80 (who owns/enforces), not P37 since it gives no penalty itself.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. Source: 'The following penalties are at the discretion of the provost and dean or their designees.' It names who decides penalties, so P80 is kept.

units.why: Level 1 penalties are described as 'educative rather than punitive', so a first, unintentional violation is handled as a learning matter. P68 (respond educatively) fits better than P37 because the point is the educative stance.
units.resolution_why: Both coded P68, admin, when-misuse, informs. Unit_stance differed (A neutral, B permit); the sentence states an educative aim and does not permit AI use, so neutral. Both noted it covers Level 1 only and is not AI-specific.

units.why: Level 1 conditions: 'lack of knowledge' and 'not intentional and ... first offense', which treats good-faith first offenses as lower level. It defines the level rather than the response, so P37 (penalty escalation by offense) is chosen over P68.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. Source: 'The violation is not intentional and is the first offense.' It states a criterion for Level 1, the lowest penalty tier, which applies to AI misuse; kept as P37 with a fit_note since it defines a level rather than a penalty.

units.why: Level 1 lists concrete penalties such as 'requiring the student to rewrite a paper for a minimally passing grade', which is a stated penalty in advance (P37).
units.resolution_why: Only A coded the Level 1 penalty list as its own unit (B had one combined P37 unit for Levels 2 to 4). Source lists makeup, rewrite for a minimally passing grade, ethics knowledge, and community service. Kept as its own unit because each level is a distinct set of sanctions. The normalized policy matches the list.

units.policy: Level 1 penalties may include making up the assignment, rewriting a paper for a minimally passing grade, acquiring specific knowledge related to ethics, and community service for a specified number of hours.

units.why: Level 2 penalties include 'assigning a failing grade in the course', a concrete sanction listed in advance for more serious, partly intentional violations (P37).
units.resolution_why: Both coded P37 for the penalty scale (B in one combined unit for Levels 2 to 4, A one unit per level). Source lists distinct Level 2 penalties; the normalized policy follows the source list. Level 3 and Level 4 are separate A units below since each level is a separate rule. B's actor was student and A's admin; penalties are decided by the provost, dean and associate dean, so admin.

units.policy: Level 2 penalties may include an academic warning of up to one year, no credit for the work, a failing grade in the course, and a short paper on the ethical issues of the violation.

units.why: Level 3 penalties include 'suspension from the University for one or more semesters', listed in advance for intentional, premeditated violations (P37).
units.resolution_why: Only A coded Level 3 separately. Source lists probation, failing grade, restitution, suspension and withdrawal of funding. Policy matches the source.

units.policy: Level 3 penalties may include academic probation, a failing grade in the course, restitution for damages, suspension from the University for one or more semesters, and withdrawal of University funding.

units.why: Level 4 penalties include 'revocation of an awarded degree' and 'dismissal from the University', the most severe stated sanctions (P37).

notes: Merged from coders A and B. Single university-layer document; only the Misuse of AI paragraph and one procedural sentence are AI-specific, the rest is the general integrity penalty and process system that governs AI cases. Fit notes from both coders are kept (B's P41 and P62 notes merged into the P61 unit). A's one-week/inform-student unit was split into two. No school or computing policy found.
